title: "Bring All Your Cash to Bolivia," They Said. La Paz Would Like a Word.
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_markdown:
Bolivia attracts a certain kind of nomad: the one who has already done Medellin and Mexico City and wants somewhere with real edges. And with that crowd comes a thick layer of received wisdom about money. Some of it is still true. A surprising amount of it froze around 2018 and never got updated. If you are planning a month in La Paz, a stretch in Santa Cruz, or a loop through the salar, here are the beliefs you will hear in every hostel kitchen, and what is actually going on in 2026.


### "Bolivia runs entirely on cash"


Half true, which makes it the most dangerous kind of myth. Nationally, yes, Bolivia is still a cash-heavy economy, and if you never leave the mercado circuit you could believe nothing has changed. But in La Paz and Santa Cruz, QR Simple has been quietly spreading across counters. It is the interbank QR standard that lets a customer scan a code and pay straight from their account, and you will now spot the printed codes taped next to the till at cafes in Sopocachi, at almuerzo spots, at pharmacies, even at some market stalls where the vendor keeps the laminated QR clipped to the awning.


The mistake travelers make is treating this as trivia. It is not. Every QR Simple code you can pay is one less trip to an ATM, and in Bolivia, ATM trips are the actual pain point, which brings us to the next myth.


### "I'll just pull cash from ATMs as I go"


This is the belief that strands people. In La Paz, Santa Cruz, and Cochabamba you can generally find machines that accept foreign cards, though not every machine and not every bank, so expect some walking. Outside the big cities, the picture changes fast. Few ATMs accept foreign cards once you leave the major urban centers, and the towns where nomads actually want to linger, Copacabana on Lake Titicaca, Uyuni before the salt flats, Rurrenabaque on the edge of the Amazon, are exactly the places where your card is most likely to be politely rejected by every machine in town.


The correction is simple but non-negotiable: treat the big cities as your cash refueling stations. Withdraw what you need for a rural stretch before you get on the bus, not after you arrive. Bolivia rewards the traveler who thinks in two economies, urban and everything else, a split that will feel familiar if you read our piece on[planning for Mongolia's city and countryside money divide](https://moretapay.com/blog/mongolia-two-economies-qr-ulaanbaatar-cash-countryside-nomad-guide-2026-2026-09-09) . Same logic, different hemisphere.


### "QR Simple is only for Bolivians with local bank accounts"


This is the myth that costs foreigners the most convenience. Locals pay by scanning QR Simple codes from their banking apps, and travelers assume that door is closed to them because they cannot open a Bolivian account on a tourist stamp. The account part is true. The conclusion is not.


Moreta Pay lets you scan those same QR Simple codes with your phone. You top up a wallet from your home bank (US bank connection via Plaid or ACH, European SEPA, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or an international card, in your own currency. At the counter, you scan the merchant's code, see the amount in bolivianos, the exchange rate, and the merchant's name on one screen, and confirm. The merchant gets paid instantly in local currency, exactly as if a local had paid, and you never touched an ATM. For a nomad splitting a month between La Paz coworking cafes and Santa Cruz lunch spots, that quietly removes most of the cash anxiety from daily life.


### "Cards work fine in the cities, so who needs QR"


Your Visa will work at the hotel front desk, the upscale restaurant in Zona Sur, and the big supermarket. That is roughly where the card story ends. The places you actually spend daily as a nomad, the salteña window, the juice lady at Mercado Lanza, the corner tienda selling you water and coca leaves before a hike, do not run card terminals and never will. Many of them do, however, have a QR Simple code, because for a small Bolivian merchant a printed code costs nothing.


So the practical hierarchy in La Paz and Santa Cruz in 2026 looks like this: QR where you see a code, cash where you do not, and your physical card reserved for hotels and the occasional big-ticket purchase. Cards also come with the usual foreign transaction fee question marks, whereas a wallet like Moreta Pay shows you the FX rate before you confirm, so the price on the screen is the price you pay.


### "Bolivia works like Peru, I just came from there"


Understandable, and wrong in the details. Crossing from Puno to Copacabana does not carry your payment habits with you. Peru's everyday QR world revolves around its own apps and rails, which we unpacked in[our Peru money myths guide](https://moretapay.com/blog/peru-money-myths-yape-plin-qr-visitor-guide-2026-2026-09-04) , and none of that infrastructure follows you across the border. In Bolivia the standard to look for is QR Simple, the merchant density is lower, and the cash fallback matters more. Reset your assumptions at the border along with your SIM card.


### "Everything online has to be paid in person anyway"


Bolivia's e-commerce scene is smaller than its neighbors', but nomads still book flights, buses, and rooms online, and increasingly those checkouts offer a QR payment option. Where a platform presents a QR code at checkout, the same scan-and-confirm flow works: Moreta Pay handles QR-based online payments the way it handles a code taped to a cafe counter. It will not cover every Bolivian website, but when the QR option appears, you are not locked out just because your bank is in Denver or Dublin.


### What a sane Bolivia setup actually looks like


Strip away the myths and the plan is short. One: land in La Paz or Santa Cruz with a funded wallet so your first coffee, cab, and SIM top-up do not depend on finding a cooperative ATM at altitude while jet-lagged. Two: pay by QR Simple everywhere you see a code in the big cities, and let your cash pile shrink slower. Three: before any trip to Uyuni, Copacabana, the Yungas, or anywhere smaller than Cochabamba, withdraw enough bolivianos to cover the whole leg, then add a margin, because the countryside is genuinely cash country and no app changes that yet. Four: keep a card for hotels and emergencies.


That is the whole system. Bolivia is not the cash-only fortress the 2018 blog posts describe, and it is not cashless either. It is a country in the middle of a transition, and the travelers who thrive are the ones who play both sides of it.[Set up Moreta Pay before you fly](https://moretapay.com/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=country-seo) and you arrive already speaking the QR half of Bolivia's money language, with the cash half reduced to a manageable habit instead of a daily scavenger hunt.
